questions.title: What is React and what problem does it solve?
questions.quick: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of components. It is declarative: I describe what the UI should look like for the current state, and React works out how to update the DOM when that state changes. It is only the view layer, so routing, data fetching and global state come from the ecosystem or a framework. I use it for reusable component architecture and for interactive, data-driven applications that grow over time.
questions.revision: React is a declarative, component-based UI library: you describe the UI for a given state and React updates the DOM when state changes.
questions.detailed:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from small, reusable pieces called components. Its core idea is **declarative rendering**: you write code that describes what the UI should look like for a given state, and React is responsible for making the browser match that description.

## How it works

- A component is a function that takes inputs (props) and returns a description of UI (React elements).
- When state or props change, React calls the component again and gets a new description.
- React compares the new description with the previous one and applies only the necessary changes to the DOM.

Compare this with imperative DOM code, where you manually find nodes and mutate them in the right order:

```js
// Imperative: you manage every DOM step
const el = document.querySelector('#count');
el.textContent = String(Number(el.textContent) + 1);
```

```jsx
// Declarative: you describe the result for the current state
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Clicked {count} times</button>;
}
```

## What React is not

React is a library, not a full framework. It focuses on rendering. Routing, data fetching, forms, and build tooling come from other libraries or from frameworks built on React such as Next.js or Remix.

## Where it fits well

- Highly interactive, stateful interfaces (dashboards, configurators, search and filter experiences).
- Large applications where many teams need shared, consistent building blocks.
- Applications that consume APIs and need predictable state-to-UI mapping.

## Common misconceptions

- "React is just the Virtual DOM." The Virtual DOM is an implementation detail; the real value is the component and declarative model.
- "React is always faster than plain JavaScript." It trades some overhead for maintainability; performance still needs deliberate design.

questions.title: Why use React instead of plain JavaScript?
questions.quick: Plain JavaScript can build any UI, but as an app grows, hand-written DOM updates become hard to keep in sync with data. React gives me components for reuse, a predictable one-way flow from state to UI, and an efficient update mechanism. It also brings a large ecosystem, good tooling and testing support, and clear ownership boundaries for teams. The trade-off is a build step, a learning curve and extra runtime weight, so for a small static page I may not need it.
questions.revision: React replaces manual DOM syncing with components and state-driven rendering, improving reuse and maintainability at the cost of tooling, bundle weight and a learning curve.
questions.detailed:
You can build any interface with plain JavaScript, so the real question is when React's model pays for itself. The short answer: as UI complexity and team size grow, keeping the DOM synchronized with data by hand becomes the main source of bugs.

## What React adds

- **Componentization**: UI is split into focused, reusable units that own their markup and behavior.
- **State-driven rendering**: the UI is a function of state, so you stop tracking which DOM nodes to update.
- **Efficient updates**: React batches changes and applies only the necessary DOM operations.
- **Ecosystem and tooling**: routing, data fetching, testing libraries, dev tools and design-system integrations are widely available.
- **Team scalability**: shared component APIs and conventions give teams clear boundaries and consistent patterns.

## Comparison

| Concern | Plain JavaScript | React |
|---|---|---|
| Updating UI | Manually query and mutate DOM | Change state; React updates the DOM |
| Reuse | Ad hoc functions or templates | Composable components with props |
| Consistency across a large codebase | Depends on team discipline | Established conventions and patterns |
| Initial setup | None | Build tooling and a runtime library |
| Small static pages | Often simpler | Usually overkill |

## Trade-offs to acknowledge

- A build pipeline, JSX transform and a runtime add weight and complexity.
- Poorly structured React apps can still be slow or tangled; the library does not enforce good architecture.
- For mostly static, content-heavy pages, server-rendered HTML with a little JavaScript can be the better fit.

## Practical example

A dealer-search page with filters, a result list, a map and saved favorites has many pieces of state that affect several views. Expressing each as a component that renders from shared state is far easier to reason about than coordinating dozens of manual DOM updates.

questions.title: What is JSX and how does it work?
questions.quick: JSX is a syntax extension that lets me write markup-like structures inside JavaScript or TypeScript. It is not HTML and the browser never sees it. A compiler such as Babel, SWC or esbuild turns each JSX tag into a function call that creates a React element, which is just a plain object describing the UI. Because it is JavaScript, I can embed expressions in braces, use className instead of class, and must return a single root or a fragment.
questions.revision: JSX is syntax sugar compiled to function calls that create React element objects; it is JavaScript, not HTML, so expressions go in braces.
questions.detailed:
JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write markup-like code inside JavaScript. It is not HTML and it is not understood by the browser. A build tool (Babel, SWC, esbuild, TypeScript) compiles it into regular JavaScript before it runs. ## What it compiles to Each JSX tag becomes a call that creates a **React element**, a lightweight object describing what should appear on screen. ```jsx const element =

Hello, {name}

; // With the modern JSX transform, roughly equivalent to: // jsx('h1', { className: 'title', children: ['Hello, ', name] }) ``` The result is an object with a type (like `'h1'` or a component function) and props. It is not a DOM node. ## Key rules - **Expressions in braces**: `{user.name}`, `{items.length > 0 && }`. Statements such as `if` or `for` are not allowed inline. - **Single root**: return one parent element or a fragment (`<>...`). - **Attribute naming**: DOM attributes use camelCase and some differ from HTML, e.g. `className`, `htmlFor`, `onClick`. - **Components start with a capital letter**; lowercase tags are treated as built-in DOM elements. - **Escaping by default**: values interpolated in braces are escaped, which helps against injection of markup (it is not a complete XSS defense). ## Common mistakes - Treating JSX as a template language and expecting loops or conditionals as directives. You use ordinary JavaScript such as `map` and ternaries. - Rendering an object directly (e.g. `{user}`) which throws; render its fields instead. - Using `0 && `, which renders the number 0. ## Is JSX required? No. You can call `createElement` or `jsx` directly, but JSX is far more readable. It also works with TypeScript for type-checked props.

questions.title: What is a React component, and how do function and class components differ?
questions.quick: A component is a reusable unit of UI and behavior; it takes props and returns React elements describing what to render. Modern React uses function components, with hooks supplying state, effects and context. Class components extend React.Component and use lifecycle methods; they are still supported and appear mainly in legacy code, and error boundaries are the main case that still needs a class. I keep each component focused on one responsibility and move data fetching and business logic out of presentation code.
questions.revision: A component is a reusable function (or class) from props to UI. Prefer function components with hooks; classes remain supported, mostly legacy, plus error boundaries.
questions.detailed:
A component is an independent, reusable piece of UI that accepts inputs (props), can own some state, and returns a description of what to render. ## Function components ```jsx function UserCard({ name, role }) { return (

{name}

{role}

); } ``` They are plain functions. Hooks such as `useState` and `useEffect` give them state, side effects and access to context. ## Class components ```jsx class UserCard extends React.Component { state = { expanded: false }; render() { return

{this.props.name}

; } } ``` They use `this.state`, `this.props` and lifecycle methods such as `componentDidMount`. ## Comparison | Aspect | Function component | Class component | |---|---|---| | State | `useState`, `useReducer` | `this.state`, `setState` | | Side effects | `useEffect` | Lifecycle methods | | Logic reuse | Custom hooks | HOCs, render props | | Boilerplate | Low | Higher (`this` binding, lifecycle split) | | Status | Recommended default | Supported, mostly legacy | ## Practical guidance - Default to function components; class components are not deprecated but new features target hooks. - Error boundaries are the notable case that still requires a class component (React does not provide a hook equivalent), though libraries such as react-error-boundary wrap this. - Keep components small and single-purpose. Separate presentational components from data access and business rules so they are easier to test and reuse. - Component names must start with a capital letter so React treats them as components, not DOM tags. ## Common mistakes - Defining a component inside another component's body, which creates a new component type every render and resets its state. - Letting one component handle fetching, transformation, layout and formatting.

questions.title: What are props in React?
questions.quick: Props are the inputs a parent passes to a child component, similar to function arguments. They let one component be configured and reused in many places. Props are read-only: a child must never mutate them, and if it needs to change something it calls a function the parent passed down, such as an onChange callback. Props can be any JavaScript value including objects, functions and other elements, and the special children prop lets components wrap nested content.
questions.revision: Props are read-only inputs from parent to child. A child never mutates them; it requests changes by calling callback props.
questions.detailed:
Props (short for properties) are the inputs a parent component passes to a child. They make components configurable and reusable, much like arguments make functions reusable.

```jsx
function UserCard({ name, onSelect }) {
  return <button onClick={() => onSelect(name)}>{name}</button>;
}

function UserList() {
  return <UserCard name="Asha" onSelect={(n) => console.log(n)} />;
}
```

## Key characteristics

- **Read-only**: a component must behave like a pure function with respect to its props. Do not assign to `props.name` or mutate a prop object.
- **One-way data flow**: data goes down from parent to child. To communicate upward, the parent passes a callback and the child calls it.
- **Any value**: strings, numbers, objects, arrays, functions, JSX elements.
- **`children`**: content placed between a component's tags arrives as `props.children`, which enables composition.
- **Defaults**: use default parameter values in destructuring (`{ size = 'md' }`).

## Why mutation is a bug

React decides what to re-render based on state and props identity. A child silently mutating a prop object changes data the parent owns without the parent knowing, so the UI can show stale or inconsistent values and bugs become hard to trace.

## Typing props

In TypeScript, define an interface or type for props so incorrect usage fails at compile time, which is especially useful for shared design-system components.

## Common mistakes

- Copying a prop into state (`useState(props.value)`) and then expecting it to follow later prop changes. The initial value is only read on first render.
- Passing too many props ("prop drilling") through components that do not use them; consider composition or context.
- Passing a new inline object or function each render to a memoized child and defeating its memoization.

questions.title: What is state in React?
questions.quick: State is data a component owns and remembers between renders that can change over time. When I call the setter, React schedules a re-render so the UI reflects the new value. Typical examples are form input values, a loading flag, a selected filter or whether a modal is open. State is private to the component instance unless I pass it down as props, and I try to keep it minimal and avoid storing anything I can compute from other state or props.
questions.revision: State is component-owned data that persists across renders; calling its setter schedules a re-render. Keep it minimal and derive everything else.
questions.detailed:
State is data that a component owns and remembers between renders, and that can change in response to user actions or events. Updating state tells React to render the component again with the new value.

```jsx
function SearchBox() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  return (
    <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
  );
}
```

## Why not an ordinary variable?

Local variables reset on every render, and changing them does not trigger a re-render. State is preserved by React between renders and its setter schedules the update.

## What belongs in state

- Form field values, selected tabs and filters
- Loading, error and open/closed flags
- Data that the user can change and that affects what is shown

## What does not belong in state

- **Derived values** such as a filtered list or a full name; compute them during render.
- **Values that never affect rendering**; a ref may be better.
- **Duplicated data** that is already in props or other state, which tends to drift out of sync.

## Principles

1. **Minimal state**: store the smallest representation and derive the rest.
2. **Lift state up**: if two components need the same state, move it to their closest common parent.
3. **Treat it as a snapshot**: within one render, the state variable has a fixed value; setting it does not change the current render's variable.
4. **Update immutably**: create new objects or arrays instead of mutating.

## Common mistakes

- Reading state right after calling the setter and expecting the new value.
- Storing a whole API response alongside a copy of the same data in another state variable.

questions.title: What is the difference between props and state?
questions.quick: Props are inputs passed in from a parent; the component treats them as read-only. State is data the component owns and can change through its setter, which triggers a re-render. Props configure a component, state drives its own dynamic behavior. Both can trigger renders when they change, and a parent's state often becomes a child's props. If two components need the same data, I lift the state to their common parent and pass it down as props.
questions.revision: Props come from the parent and are read-only; state is owned by the component and changed via setters. A parent's state becomes a child's props.
questions.detailed:
Both props and state are plain data that influence what a component renders, and a change in either causes a re-render. The difference is **ownership**.

| | Props | State |
|---|---|---|
| Owner | Parent component | The component itself |
| Mutable by the component? | No (read-only) | Yes, via its setter |
| Purpose | Configure and feed data | Track values that change over time |
| Who triggers a change | The parent re-renders with new values | An event or effect calls the setter |
| Initial value | Passed at usage site | Set in `useState(initial)` |

## How they work together

State in one component commonly becomes props in another:

```jsx
function Parent() {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState(null);   // state owned here
  return <VehicleList selected={selected} onSelect={setSelected} />; // props below
}
```

`Parent` owns `selected`. `VehicleList` cannot assign it; it calls `onSelect` to ask the parent to change it. This is one-way data flow with events flowing up.

## Deciding where data lives

1. Does it change over time and affect the UI? It is state or derived from state.
2. Who needs it? If only one component, keep it there. If siblings need it, lift it to the nearest common parent.
3. Can it be computed from other props or state? Then it should not be state.

## Common mistakes

- Copying props into state, which creates two sources of truth.
- Mutating a prop object in a child.
- Putting everything in a top-level component or global store when local state would do, causing broad re-renders.

questions.title: How does React render a component when state or props change?
questions.quick: Rendering means React calling my component function to get a description of the UI. When state or props change, React re-runs the component, producing a new element tree, then compares it with the previous tree. In the commit phase it applies only the needed changes to the DOM, and then runs effects. Rendering and DOM updating are separate: a component can render without any DOM change, and by default a parent render also re-renders its children.
questions.revision: State or prop change triggers render (call component, build element tree), then reconciliation diffs it, then commit applies minimal DOM changes and effects run.
questions.detailed:
In React, "rendering" does **not** mean painting pixels. It means React calling your component function to calculate what the UI should look like. The process has three stages.

{{diagram:flow}}

## 1. Trigger

A render is triggered by the initial mount, or by a state update (a setter call) in a component. Props changes cause children to render because their parent rendered.

## 2. Render phase

React calls the component function. The returned element tree is compared (reconciled) against the previous one to find what changed. This phase must be **pure**: same props and state in, same JSX out, with no side effects. In Strict Mode during development React may call components twice to help reveal impure code.

## 3. Commit phase

React applies the minimal set of DOM changes, then runs layout effects and after paint, passive effects (`useEffect`).

## Important consequences

- **A render is not a DOM update.** If the output is identical, the DOM is not touched.
- **Parent renders re-render children by default**, even if the props did not change, unless the child is wrapped in `React.memo` (and its props are stable).
- **State updates are batched** and may be processed together, so many setter calls in one event handler produce a single render.
- **Rendering must be cheap and pure**. Fetching, subscriptions and mutations belong in event handlers or effects.

## Common mistakes

- Putting side effects in the component body.
- Assuming a re-render means the DOM was rebuilt.
- Assuming the state variable changes within the current render after calling the setter.

diagrams.title: React render lifecycle
diagrams.alt: A state or props change triggers a render in which React calls the component; the new element tree is reconciled against the previous tree; the commit phase updates the DOM and then runs effects.

questions.title: What is the Virtual DOM?
questions.quick: The Virtual DOM is the idea of keeping a lightweight in-memory description of the UI, the tree of React elements, and comparing the new tree with the previous one to decide what real DOM changes are needed. It lets me write declaratively without hand-managing DOM updates. It is not inherently faster than hand-optimized DOM code; its benefit is that it makes updates predictable and usually efficient enough. React's own docs rarely use the term, preferring element tree and reconciliation.
questions.revision: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory element tree React diffs against the previous one to apply minimal real DOM changes; it enables declarative UI, not magic speed.
questions.detailed:
The Virtual DOM is a programming concept: the UI is represented as lightweight JavaScript objects (React elements) kept in memory. On each render React produces a new tree, compares it with the previous one, and applies only the differences to the real DOM. ## Why it exists Real DOM operations are comparatively expensive and, more importantly, hand-written updates are error-prone. With the Virtual DOM approach you describe the whole UI for the current state and let the library figure out the minimal change set. ```jsx // Two renders with different state produce two element trees: // before:
  • A
  • B
// after:
  • A
  • B
  • C
// React's diff: append one
  • C
    • . The existing items are left alone. ``` ## What it is not - **Not a copy of the browser DOM.** Elements are small descriptions, not nodes with layout or styles. - **Not automatically faster than careful manual DOM code.** A hand-tuned update touching exactly one node can beat any diff. The win is developer productivity and predictable, generally good performance. - **Not the only approach.** Some frameworks use compile-time analysis or fine-grained reactivity instead of tree diffing. ## Related concepts - **Fiber** is React's internal data structure and scheduler that enables interruptible rendering. You rarely need to know it in detail, but it explains how concurrent features work. - **Reconciliation** is the diffing algorithm that operates on the element trees. ## Interview tips Avoid claiming "Virtual DOM makes React fast." A more accurate statement is that it enables a declarative model with efficient-enough updates, and that performance problems usually come from rendering too much work, not from the DOM diff itself.

questions.title: What is reconciliation in React?
questions.quick: Reconciliation is how React compares the previous element tree with the new one to decide what to update. It uses two heuristics: elements of different types produce different trees, so React tears down the old subtree and builds a new one; and for lists, keys identify which items are the same across renders. If the type and position match, React reuses the existing instance and updates its props, preserving state. This is why stable keys and consistent structure matter.
questions.revision: Reconciliation diffs old and new element trees: same type and position updates in place and keeps state; different type remounts; keys identify list items.
questions.detailed:
Reconciliation is the algorithm React uses to compare the previous element tree with the new one and work out the minimum set of changes to apply. A fully general tree diff is too expensive, so React relies on two practical assumptions.

{{diagram:diff}}

## The rules

1. **Different element types produce different trees.** If a `<div>` becomes a `<section>`, or `<Form>` becomes `<Panel>`, React unmounts the old subtree (destroying its state) and mounts a new one.
2. **Same type at the same position updates in place.** React keeps the DOM node or component instance, updates changed props or attributes, and recurses into the children. State is preserved.
3. **Keys identify children in lists.** With keys, React can match items across renders even when they move.

## Practical implications

- **State is tied to position and type in the tree.** Conditionally rendering a different component at the same spot resets state; rendering the same component keeps it.
- **Changing a key forces a remount.** This is a deliberate technique to reset a component's state, e.g. `<ProfileForm key={userId} />`.
- **Defining components inside other components** creates a new type every render, so React remounts them every time.

```jsx
// State resets when switching because the types differ
{isAdmin ? <AdminPanel /> : <UserPanel />}

// State is preserved because the type and position are the same
{isAdmin ? <Panel mode="admin" /> : <Panel mode="user" />}
```

## Common mistakes

- Using random or index keys that break identity.
- Wrapping elements conditionally so a stable component moves in the tree and loses state.
- Assuming reconciliation updates the DOM; it only decides what should change, and the commit phase applies it.

diagrams.title: Reconciliation decisions
diagrams.alt: React compares the old and new element at a position. If the types differ it unmounts the old subtree and mounts a new one; if the types are the same it keeps the instance, updates props, and recurses into children.

questions.title: What are keys in React lists, and why should you avoid array indexes as keys?
questions.quick: A key gives each list item a stable identity so React can match items between renders and tell which were added, removed or moved. I use a stable unique id from the data, such as a database id. Array indexes are risky when the list can be reordered, filtered or have items inserted, because the index then points to a different item and React can attach the wrong component state, such as an input's text, to the wrong row. Random keys are worse, since they remount everything each render.
questions.revision: Keys give list items stable identity for reconciliation. Use unique stable ids, not indexes or random values, when lists reorder, filter or change.
questions.detailed:
A key is a special attribute that tells React which element in a list corresponds to which item across renders. It lets reconciliation correctly detect additions, removals and reordering.

```jsx
{users.map((user) => (
  <UserCard key={user.id} user={user} />
))}
```

Keys must be unique among siblings (not globally) and stable between renders. They are not passed to the component as a prop.

## Why indexes can break things

If the key is the index, the identity belongs to the **position**, not the **data**. When the list changes, the same key now refers to a different item.

Suppose a list of editable rows, each with an uncontrolled input, and you delete the first row:

- With **id keys**, React removes the first row's component, and the remaining rows keep their own input text.
- With **index keys**, React sees keys 0 and 1 remain and the last key vanishes. It keeps the first component instance (with the deleted row's typed text) and feeds it the next item's props. State ends up attached to the wrong row. Effects and animations can misbehave similarly.

## When index keys are acceptable

The list is static, never reordered or filtered, and items have no local state and no stable ids. Even then, an id is better if available.

## Choosing keys

- Prefer ids from the data (database id, SKU, slug).
- If items have no ids, generate one once when the data is created or loaded, not during render.
- Avoid `Math.random()` or `crypto.randomUUID()` inside the render, since every render produces new keys and forces every item to remount.

## Other uses

Changing a key deliberately resets a component's state, which is a clean way to reset a form when the selected entity changes.
